question.text: A bank has issued floating-rate loans and is concerned about rates declining, which would reduce its interest income. How can interest rate options help?

answer.text: Buy interest rate put options (or a floor) to establish a minimum rate of return on the floating-rate portfolio
Sell interest rate call options to generate premium income to offset lower rates
Buy interest rate call options to benefit from rate declines
Write interest rate put options to earn premium as rates decline

explanation.text: The Logic: A bank with floating-rate loans earns interest that rises and falls with the reference rate, so falling rates compress its income. Buying interest-rate puts (or, equivalently, an interest-rate floor — conceptually a strip of put options on the rate, one per reset period) pays off when the reference rate falls below the strike, restoring lost interest and effectively setting a minimum rate of return on the floating-rate portfolio. The Trap: Selling calls generates a one-off premium but provides no protection if rates fall — and exposes the bank to losses if rates rise. Buying calls benefits from rate increases, the opposite of what is needed here. Writing puts collects premium initially but adds, rather than offsets, the loss from falling rates. Note: The cited workbook (NISM Series IV, pages 21, 142, 154, 161, 166, 182) covers Floating Rate Bond floors protecting investors from falling rates, Black-model pricing of caps/floors, and OTC IRO products including caps/floors, but does not explicitly characterize a floor as a strip of puts used by a bank with floating-rate loans to set a minimum return. The framing above is general interest-rate-derivatives knowledge.
